"Pass off" is a phrasal verb — a verb combined with a small word ("off") that together create a meaning quite different from the words on their own. "Pass" alone means to move or go by. But "pass off" opens up into four distinct, separate meanings.

Meaning 1 — To Pretend Something Is What It's Not (Most Common)

This is the meaning you'll encounter most often. When someone "passes something off as" something else, they are deceiving people — presenting a fake, inferior, or false thing as if it were real, genuine, or better.

The pattern: pass [something / someone] off as [something / someone]

Examples:

  • "He passed off a cheap watch as a luxury brand."
  • "The student tried to pass off someone else's essay as her own."
  • "The salesman passed the old car off as brand new."
  • "She passed herself off as a doctor to get access to the hospital."

The soul of this meaning is deception. There is always something false being presented as real. The word "as" is essential here — it connects what the thing actually is to what it is being falsely claimed to be.

You can use this about objects, ideas, or even people (including yourself). "Passing yourself off as" someone means pretending to be that person or role.

Meaning 2 — To Dismiss or Brush Something Aside

Here, "pass something off" means to treat something as unimportant and not give it the attention it deserves. The person casually pushes it away, often to avoid dealing with it seriously.

The pattern: pass [something] off (+ as [something])

Examples:

  • "She passed off his rude comment as a joke."
  • "He passed off the doctor's warning as an overreaction."
  • "Don't pass off their complaints — they are serious."
  • "She passed the whole incident off as nothing."

This is very close in meaning to "brush off" or "shrug off." The person refuses to take something — a criticism, a warning, a strange event — seriously. They dismiss it and move on.

Note: Meanings 1 and 2 can sometimes look similar. The difference is intention:

  • Meaning 1 = you are actively trying to deceive someone else.
  • Meaning 2 = you are dismissing something, for your own convenience or peace of mind, sometimes even deceiving yourself.

Meaning 3 — (Of an Event) To Happen and End in a Certain Way

When an event "passes off" in a particular way, it means the event took place and concluded in that manner. This meaning is about how smoothly or how well something went from start to finish.

The pattern: [event] + passes off + adverb OR "without any _"

Examples:

  • "The wedding passed off beautifully."
  • "The protest passed off without any violence."
  • "The annual conference passed off without a single problem."
  • "Thankfully, the surgery passed off well."

You will almost always find an adverb (beautifully, smoothly, quietly) or a phrase like "without any trouble" or "without incident" with this meaning. It rarely appears on its own. This usage is more common in British English.

Meaning 4 — (Of a Pain or Feeling) To Gradually Fade Away

In this meaning, "pass off" describes a physical sensation or feeling that slowly disappears on its own.

The pattern: [feeling / pain / sensation] + passes off

Examples:

  • "The headache passed off after I took some rest."
  • "Don't worry — the dizziness will pass off in a few minutes."
  • "The nausea passed off once she got some fresh air."
  • "His anger passed off by the evening."

This is similar to "wear off" or "subside." The feeling doesn't stop suddenly — it fades gradually over time.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

The object position — separable vs. inseparable

For Meanings 1 and 2, "pass off" is a separable phrasal verb. This means the object can either go between "pass" and "off," or it can come after the whole phrase:

  • "He passed the fake coin off as genuine." ✓
  • "He passed off the fake coin as genuine." ✓

Both sentences are correct. However, there is one strict rule:

When the object is a pronoun (it, him, her, them, yourself, myself), it must always go in the middle — between "pass" and "off":

  • "He passed it off as genuine." ✓
  • "He passed off it as genuine." ✗ — This is wrong.

Think of it this way: a pronoun cannot follow "off." It must sit between the two words.

For Meanings 3 and 4, "pass off" behaves as a single, unseparated unit. The event or feeling simply "passes off" — nothing goes in between:

  • "The ceremony passed off smoothly." ✓ (not: "passed smoothly off")
  • "The pain passed off." ✓
The Word "As" — When Is It Required?

In Meaning 1, the word "as" is almost always required. Without it, the sentence sounds incomplete or wrong:

  • "She passed the bag off as a designer original." ✓
  • "She passed the bag off a designer original." ✗

In Meaning 2, "as" is optional. You can say:

  • "He passed off her concerns as paranoia." (with "as")
  • "He passed off her concerns." (without "as" — also fine)

In Meanings 3 and 4, "as" is not used.

Knowing synonyms helps you understand the exact shade of meaning more deeply.

Meaning 1 (deceive): palm off, foist off, misrepresent as, disguise as
Meaning 2 (dismiss): brush off, shrug off, wave aside, dismiss
Meaning 3 (event ending well): go off, proceed, transpire, unfold
Meaning 4 (pain fading): wear off, subside, fade, die down, dissipate

Mistake 1 — Forgetting "as" in Meaning 1:

  • ✗ "He passed off the letter a forgery."
  • ✓ "He passed off the letter as a forgery."

Mistake 2 — Putting a pronoun after "off":

  • ✗ "She passed off it as harmless."
  • ✓ "She passed it off as harmless."

Mistake 3 — Confusing "pass off" with similar phrases:

  • "Pass out" = to faint, or to distribute something ("She passed out the exam papers.")
  • "Pass up" = to miss or decline an opportunity ("He passed up a great job offer.")
  • "Pass away" = to die (a gentle way of saying it)

These are completely separate phrases with no connection to "pass off."
One Final Thought: The Thread That Runs Through All Four Meanings

If you look closely, you'll notice a quiet common thread: in each meaning, something is either not fully real or not fully present.

  • In Meaning 1, a fake thing is presented as real — so the "real" label is false.
  • In Meaning 2, a real concern is treated as nothing — so its importance is pushed away.
  • In Meaning 3, an event simply happens and is done — it has passed through existence.
  • In Meaning 4, a sensation fades — it is slowly moving out of existence.

"Pass off" always involves something moving away from the center — away from truth, away from importance, away from attention, or away from the present moment. Understanding this helps you feel the phrase, not just memorize it.
